sciXsBallStk: A ball-and-stick model has 1 H ball + 1 Cl ball joined by sticks. Which formula does it show?
One hydrogen atom bonded to one chlorine atom is hydrogen chloride, HCl.
A ball-and-stick model has 1 C ball + 1 O ball joined by sticks. Which formula does it show?
One carbon atom and one oxygen atom make carbon monoxide, CO.
A ball-and-stick model has 1 N ball + 2 O balls joined by sticks. Which formula does it show?
One nitrogen and two oxygen atoms give the formula NO₂.
A ball-and-stick model has 2 N balls + 1 O ball joined by sticks. Which formula does it show?
Two nitrogen atoms and one oxygen atom give the formula N₂O.
A ball-and-stick model has 1 S ball + 2 O balls joined by sticks. Which formula does it show?
One sulfur atom with two oxygen atoms is sulfur dioxide, SO₂.
A ball-and-stick model has 1 S ball + 3 O balls joined by sticks. Which formula does it show?
One sulfur atom with three oxygen atoms is sulfur trioxide, SO₃.
A ball-and-stick model has 2 H balls + 1 S ball joined by sticks. Which formula does it show?
Two hydrogen atoms bonded to one sulfur atom give H₂S.
A ball-and-stick model has 2 Cl balls joined by sticks. Which formula does it show?
Two chlorine atoms joined together form a chlorine molecule, Cl₂.
A ball-and-stick model has 3 O balls joined by sticks. Which formula does it show?
Three oxygen atoms bonded in one molecule make ozone, O₃.
A ball-and-stick model has 1 C ball + 4 Cl balls joined by sticks. Which formula does it show?
One carbon atom bonded to four chlorine atoms gives CCl₄.
A ball-and-stick model has 2 C balls + 6 H balls joined by sticks. Which formula does it show?
Two carbon atoms and six hydrogen atoms make ethane, C₂H₆.
A ball-and-stick model has 3 C balls + 8 H balls joined by sticks. Which formula does it show?
Three carbon atoms and eight hydrogen atoms make propane, C₃H₈.
A ball-and-stick model has 2 C balls + 4 H balls joined by sticks. Which formula does it show?
Two carbon atoms and four hydrogen atoms give ethene, C₂H₄.
A ball-and-stick model has 1 H ball + 1 F ball joined by sticks. Which formula does it show?
One hydrogen atom bonded to one fluorine atom is hydrogen fluoride, HF.
A ball-and-stick model has 1 C ball + 2 S balls joined by sticks. Which formula does it show?
One carbon atom with two sulfur atoms gives carbon disulfide, CS₂.
A ball-and-stick model has 1 P ball + 3 H balls joined by sticks. Which formula does it show?
One phosphorus atom bonded to three hydrogen atoms gives PH₃.
A ball-and-stick model has 2 H balls joined by sticks. Which formula does it show?
Two hydrogen atoms bonded together form one hydrogen molecule, H₂.
A ball-and-stick model has 1 C ball + 2 H balls + 1 O ball joined by sticks. Which formula does it show?
One carbon, two hydrogen and one oxygen atom give the formula CH₂O.

1 C ball joined to 4 H balls
4 C balls joined to 1 H ball
1 C ball joined to 2 H balls
2 C balls joined to 4 H balls

Which ball-and-stick model matches the formula SO₂?
1 S ball joined to 2 O balls
2 S balls joined to 1 O ball
1 S ball joined to 3 O balls
2 S balls joined to 2 O balls
SO₂ has no subscript on S (meaning 1) and a subscript 2 on O.
Which ball-and-stick model matches the formula C₂H₆O?
2 C, 6 H and 1 O balls joined
6 C, 2 H and 1 O balls joined
2 C, 6 H and 2 O balls joined
1 C, 6 H and 2 O balls joined
The subscripts show 2 carbon, 6 hydrogen and 1 oxygen atom.
How many balls in total are in a ball-and-stick model of CO₂?
CO₂ has one carbon atom and two oxygen atoms, so the model has 3 balls.

Every particle is the same single kind of atom, so it is an element.
What does this model show? Many pairs of identical yellow-green balls joined (Cl₂)
Each molecule contains only chlorine atoms, so it is an element.

What does this model show? Water molecules (H₂O) mixed with carbon dioxide molecules (CO₂)

What does this model show? Purple and green balls alternating in a repeating grid, all bonded (NaCl)
Sodium and chlorine are chemically combined in a fixed ratio, so it is a compound.
What does this model show? Every molecule is three identical red balls joined (O₃)
Ozone contains only oxygen atoms, so it is an element.
What does this model show? Single orange balls of one kind packed in neat rows (copper)
All the balls are the same kind of atom, so the model shows an element.
What does this model show? Every molecule is one white ball joined to one green ball (HCl)
Hydrogen and chlorine atoms are bonded together, which makes a compound.
What does this model show? Separate grey balls (helium) mixed with separate pink balls (neon), none joined
Two kinds of atoms are present but not bonded, so it is a mixture of elements.
What does this model show? Many pairs of identical white balls joined (H₂)
Each molecule contains only hydrogen atoms, so it is an element.
What does this model show? Every molecule is one black ball joined to one red ball (CO)
Carbon and oxygen are bonded together, so it is a compound.
What does this model show? CH₄ molecules mixed with NH₃ molecules
Two different compounds are mixed but not bonded to each other.
What does this model show? Every molecule is eight identical yellow balls joined in a ring (S₈)
The ring contains only sulfur atoms, so it is an element.
What does this model show? Every molecule is two black balls joined to six white balls (C₂H₆)
Carbon and hydrogen atoms are bonded in each molecule, so it is a compound.
What does this model show? Every molecule is one yellow ball joined to two red balls (SO₂)
Sulfur and oxygen atoms are bonded together in each identical molecule.
What does this model show? Pairs of white balls (H₂) mixed with pairs of red balls (O₂), not bonded to each other
Hydrogen and oxygen molecules are each elements, and here they are only mixed.
What does this model show? Layers of identical black balls all joined in sheets (graphite)
Graphite contains only carbon atoms, so it is an element.
What does this model show? Every molecule is one blue ball joined to two red balls (NO₂)
Nitrogen and oxygen atoms are bonded together, so it is a compound.
What does this model show? CO₂ molecules mixed with CO molecules
Both kinds of molecules are compounds, and they are mixed rather than bonded.
A model of N₂ shows two balls joined by a stick. Why is it an element?
Both balls are the same kind of atom
The balls are joined by a stick
It is a gas at room temperature
An element contains only one kind of atom, and both balls in N₂ are nitrogen.
In a model, every molecule has two different colours of balls joined together. What must the substance be?
Different kinds of atoms chemically joined in each molecule make a compound.
sciXsRxEnergy: Which describes the energy change? Natural gas burning in a furnace
Combustion gives off heat and light to the surroundings, so it is exothermic.
Which describes the energy change? Iron slowly rusting on a bike chain
Rusting slowly releases heat as iron combines with oxygen, so it is exothermic.
Which describes the energy change? Cells breaking down glucose in cellular respiration
Respiration releases energy stored in glucose, so it is exothermic.
Which describes the energy change? A candle burning on a table
Burning wax gives off heat and light, so energy is released.
Which describes the energy change? A glow stick giving off light after it is bent
The chemicals react and release energy as light, so the reaction is exothermic.
Which describes the energy change? An acid and a base mixing and the beaker getting warm
The beaker warms because the neutralization releases energy.
Which describes the energy change? Wet concrete warming up as it hardens
The setting reaction in concrete releases heat, so it is exothermic.
Which describes the energy change? Electricity splitting water into hydrogen and oxygen
Electrolysis needs a constant input of electrical energy, so it absorbs energy.
Which describes the energy change? Citric acid and baking soda in water making the cup feel cold
The cup cools because the reaction takes in thermal energy from its surroundings.
Which describes the energy change? Limestone breaking down into lime when heated in a kiln
The limestone only breaks down while heat is continually supplied, so it is endothermic.
Which describes the energy change? Cake batter turning into cake in a hot oven
Baking reactions happen only while the batter takes in heat from the oven.
Which describes the energy change? An egg white turning solid as it cooks in a pan
The egg changes only while it absorbs heat from the pan.
Which describes the energy change? Two powders mixed in a flask that freezes to a wet board underneath
Freezing the water under the flask shows the reaction absorbed lots of thermal energy.
Which describes the energy change? A thermite reaction producing molten iron and bright sparks
The thermite reaction gives off intense heat and light, so it is exothermic.
In an endothermic reaction, the temperature of the surroundings usually…
Energy is taken in from the surroundings, so they become cooler.
In an exothermic reaction, energy is…
Exothermic reactions give off energy, often as heat or light.
Energy must be put in to pull bonded atoms apart.
Energy is given off when atoms join to form bonds.
A reaction is exothermic overall when…
forming bonds releases more energy than breaking bonds absorbs
breaking bonds absorbs more energy than forming bonds releases
no bonds are broken and no bonds are formed
the atoms in the reactants are destroyed
If more energy comes out from new bonds than went into breaking old ones, the extra is released.
During a reaction, a thermometer rises from 20 °C to 35 °C. What does this show?
A temperature rise means the reaction released thermal energy into the mixture.
During a reaction, a thermometer drops from 22 °C to 9 °C. What does this show?
A temperature drop means the reaction took thermal energy from the mixture.
What happens to the total amount of energy during a chemical reaction?
It is conserved and only changes form
It is destroyed when bonds break
It is created when bonds form
Energy cannot be created or destroyed, so it is only transferred or transformed.
sciXsSoap: Besides soap, which product forms during saponification?
Glycerol
Ethanol
Carbon dioxide
Ammonia
When fats react with a strong base, they form soap and glycerol.
The long tail of a soap molecule is made mostly of…
carbon and hydrogen atoms
sodium and chlorine atoms
oxygen atoms only
iron and copper atoms
The tail is a hydrocarbon chain, a long chain of carbon and hydrogen atoms.
How is the tail of a soap molecule described?
Hydrophobic
Hydrophilic
Radioactive
Metallic
The hydrocarbon tail is water-fearing (hydrophobic) and mixes with oils instead.
In a micelle, which way do the soap molecules' tails point?
Inward, toward the trapped oil
Outward, toward the water
Upward, toward the air only
In completely random directions
The oil-loving tails gather around the oil in the centre while the heads face the water.
Why is soap called a surfactant?
It lowers the surface tension of water
It raises the surface tension of water
It floats only on the surface
It hardens any surface it touches
Surfactants lower surface tension, helping water spread and soak into dirt.
What type of substance is lye (sodium hydroxide)?
A strong base
A strong acid
A neutral salt
A pure element
Sodium hydroxide is a strong base, which is why it can react with fats to make soap.
Soap made with potassium hydroxide instead of sodium hydroxide tends to be…
softer, often a liquid soap
harder than sodium soap
a gas at room temperature
unable to clean at all
Potassium soaps are softer and are used for many liquid soaps.
Why is homemade cold-process soap left to cure for several weeks?
To let saponification finish and water evaporate
To let the bar grow larger over time
To change the soap into an acid
To let bacteria grow and clean it
Curing gives the reaction time to use up the lye and lets extra water leave, making a milder, harder bar.
Why is the pH of most bar soap above 7?
It is made using a base
It is made using an acid
It contains only pure water
It contains lots of vinegar
Soap is made from a strong base, so it is slightly basic.
Which of these can be used to make soap?
Olive oil, coconut oil or animal fat
Motor oil, gasoline or kerosene
Sugar, salt or baking soda
Sand, clay or chalk
Saponification needs fats or oils from plants or animals, which react with a strong base.
Fats and oils used in soapmaking are mostly molecules called…
triglycerides
proteins
nucleic acids
starches
Fats and oils are triglycerides, which the base splits into soap and glycerol.
How do synthetic detergents behave differently from soap in hard water?
They do not form scum with the minerals
They form more scum than soap does
They turn the hard water into ice
They only work in very salty water
Detergents are designed so hard-water minerals do not make them form scum.
Which dissolved minerals make water "hard"?
Calcium and magnesium
Sodium and potassium
Gold and silver
Helium and neon
Calcium and magnesium ions cause water hardness and react with soap to make scum.
Why does scrubbing your hands help soap work?
It helps soap surround and lift off oily dirt
It makes the soap molecules magnetic
It heats the water up to boiling
It changes the soap into an acid
Rubbing mixes soap with the oil so micelles can form and carry dirt away.
Why can water easily rinse away a micelle full of oil?
The heads on its outside attract water
The tails on its outside attract water
The trapped oil turns into water
Micelles are heavier than water
The water-loving heads face outward, so the whole micelle is carried by the water.
How can soap destroy some viruses, such as flu viruses?
It breaks apart their fatty outer layer
It freezes them solid
It turns them into bacteria
It gives them extra nutrients
Soap tails attach to the fatty envelope of these viruses and pull it apart.
Oil and water do not mix on their own. What does soap act as when it lets them mix?
An emulsifier
A catalyst
A fuel
A magnet
An emulsifier lets oil spread through water as tiny droplets.
What forms when tallow (beef fat) reacts with lye?
Soap and glycerol
Sugar and water
Salt and carbon dioxide
Oil and vinegar
Saponification of any fat with lye gives soap and glycerol.
Which observation shows that saponification has happened?
Oil and lye become a new solid substance
The oil simply floats on top
The lye completely evaporates
The mixture turns into pure water
A new substance with new properties forms, which shows a chemical reaction.
Which part of a soap molecule dissolves in grease?
The hydrocarbon tail
The charged head
The sodium ion
The water molecule
Like dissolves like, so the non-polar hydrocarbon tail mixes into non-polar grease.
When mixing a lye solution, why is lye added to water and not water to lye?
Water added to lye can boil and splash
Lye floats and will not mix otherwise
Water turns into lye if added second
Lye freezes if water is added to it
Adding water onto lye releases heat in a small spot, which can make the caustic mixture boil and spatter.
In bar soap, which ion is usually paired with the negatively charged head of each soap molecule?
Sodium ion, Na⁺
Chloride ion, Cl⁻
Oxide ion, O²⁻
Fluoride ion, F⁻
A negative head is attracted to a positive ion, and soap made with sodium hydroxide contains Na⁺.
sciXsFlavour: What is the Maillard reaction?
A reaction of sugars and amino acids that browns food
A reaction that makes food freeze faster
A reaction that removes all salt from food
A reaction between water and metals
When sugars and amino acids are heated together they form brown colours and new flavour compounds.
Caramelization happens when…
sugar is heated and breaks into new compounds
sugar is frozen into large crystals
salt dissolves in cold water
fat is mixed with vinegar
Heating sugar breaks it down into new molecules with caramel colour and flavour.
Esters, which give many fruits their smell, form when…
an acid reacts with an alcohol
a metal reacts with water
salt is mixed with sugar
two noble gases combine
An ester forms from the reaction of a carboxylic acid with an alcohol.
Which compound gives cinnamon its flavour?
Cinnamaldehyde
Capsaicin
Caffeine
Citric acid
Cinnamaldehyde is the main flavour molecule in cinnamon bark.
Which compound gives orange and lemon peels their scent?
Limonene
Vanillin
Menthol
Capsaicin
Limonene is the main aroma molecule in citrus peel oil.
Why does mint feel cool in your mouth?
Menthol activates cold-sensing receptors
Menthol lowers your mouth to 0 °C
Mint leaves contain tiny ice crystals
Menthol blocks all of your taste buds
Menthol triggers the same nerve receptors that sense cold, even though nothing gets colder.
Which basic taste is triggered by glutamate, found in tomatoes and parmesan?
Umami
Sour
Bitter
Salty
Glutamate fits umami receptors and gives a savoury taste.
Why does food taste bland when you have a stuffy nose?
Aroma molecules can't reach smell receptors
Your tongue stops making any saliva
Food molecules become much heavier
Your taste buds fall off your tongue
Much of flavour is smell, and a blocked nose stops aroma molecules reaching the receptors.
Two forms of carvone have the same atoms but are mirror images. Why does one smell like spearmint and the other like caraway?
Their shapes fit smell receptors differently
They have different numbers of atoms
One of them contains no carbon
One is a metal and one is a gas

Which ions give salty foods their salty taste?
Sodium ions
Iron ions
Hydrogen ions
Hydroxide ions
Salty taste mainly comes from sodium ions, such as those in table salt.
Sour taste is mostly caused by…
hydrogen ions from acids
sodium ions from salts
sugars from ripe fruit
fats from cooking oils
Acids release hydrogen ions, which sour taste receptors detect.
Coffee tastes bitter partly because it contains…
caffeine
sucrose
sodium chloride
vanillin
Caffeine is a bitter-tasting compound found in coffee and tea.
Why can a tiny amount of aspartame replace much more sugar?
It activates sweet receptors far more strongly
It is far heavier than table sugar
It is made of pure table salt
It blocks all of the other tastes
Aspartame's structure triggers sweet receptors about 200 times more strongly than sugar.
Why does crushing garlic make its smell much stronger?
Crushing starts a reaction that makes allicin
Crushing turns the garlic into salt
Crushing makes the garlic much colder
Crushing removes only the garlic's water
Breaking garlic cells lets an enzyme react with a compound to form strong-smelling allicin.
Why do ripe bananas taste sweeter than green bananas?
Starch breaks down into sugars as they ripen
Sugars turn into starch as they ripen
Ripe bananas absorb sugar from the air
The peel pumps salt into the fruit
Enzymes in ripening fruit break starch into sweet-tasting sugars.
Why does a cut apple turn brown and change flavour?
Enzymes help apple compounds react with oxygen
The apple soaks up brown light
The sugar in the apple melts
The apple's water turns into salt
Exposed apple compounds react with oxygen, helped by enzymes, forming brown products.
Why does drinking milk help after eating hot peppers?
Capsaicin dissolves in fat rather than water
Milk is colder than ice cubes
Milk is a strong acid that burns it off
Milk contains extra capsaicin
Capsaicin is fat-soluble, so the fat in milk helps wash it away from receptors.
Wintergreen flavour comes from methyl salicylate. Which group of compounds is it in?
Esters
Metals
Noble gases
Minerals
Methyl salicylate is an ester, like many other fruity and minty flavour molecules.
Why does warm food usually smell stronger than cold food?
More aroma molecules evaporate when it is warm
Warm food contains many more atoms
Cold food has no molecules at all
Cold food blocks your smell receptors
Heat gives molecules more energy, so more of them escape into the air and reach your nose.
How can chemists make an artificial pineapple flavour?
By making the same flavour molecule found in pineapple
By growing whole pineapples in test tubes
By adding yellow colouring to the food
By removing every molecule from the food
Flavour depends on the molecule, so making the same molecule (an ester) gives the same flavour.
How many basic tastes do human taste receptors detect?
Five
Two
Ten
Twenty
The five basic tastes are sweet, sour, salty, bitter and umami.
Why can a bitter taste act as a warning?

Bitter foods are always too hot
All bitter foods contain salt
Bitter foods have no flavour molecules

monomers
isotopes
minerals
crystals

Which synthetic material coats many non-stick frying pans?

Kevlar
Nylon
Spandex

Kevlar
Teflon

It soaks up water like a sponge
It dissolves slowly in the rain
It is made from sheep's wool

What does "biodegradable" mean?
Can be broken down by living things
Can never be broken down at all
Is made only from metal
Melts instantly in sunlight
Biodegradable materials are broken down by organisms such as bacteria and fungi.
Why are microplastics a concern?
Tiny plastic bits build up in water and animals
They help fish grow faster and larger
They break down into clean sand quickly
They make lake water much warmer
Small plastic pieces last a long time and are swallowed by animals, harming food chains.
What are bioplastics such as PLA made from?
Plant materials such as corn starch
Melted rocks and beach sand
Salt water from the ocean
Crushed animal bones
PLA is made from sugars or starch taken from plants like corn.
Which property makes Kevlar useful in firefighters' gear?
It is very strong and heat-resistant
It is soft and dissolves in water
It conducts electricity very well
It is very heavy and brittle
Kevlar fibres are extremely strong and do not melt easily, protecting the wearer.
Recycling code 1 (PET plastic) is most often found on…
water and pop bottles
car and bike tires
glass pickle jars
aluminum soup cans
PET is the clear, light plastic used for most drink bottles.
Why do scientists develop new synthetic materials?
To meet needs natural materials can't meet as well
To make products break more easily
To use up all of Earth's fresh water
To make clothing much heavier
Synthetics can be designed to be stronger, lighter, waterproof or cheaper than natural materials.
Polystyrene foam is useful for take-out coffee cups because it…
is a good thermal insulator
conducts heat very well
is strongly magnetic
is safe to eat

Which synthetic material is used for many water pipes and window frames?
PVC
Oak
Granite
Cotton
PVC (polyvinyl chloride) is a tough, waterproof plastic made by chemical reactions.
Nylon stockings were first made to replace which natural fibre?
Silk
Wool
Cotton
Hemp
Nylon was developed in the 1930s as a cheaper substitute for silk.
What is one problem with making plastics from petroleum?

Petroleum is free and endless

Which item is made mainly of a synthetic material?
A polyester fleece jacket
A wool mitten
A cotton T-shirt
A leather belt

Plastic shopping bags are usually made of which synthetic polymer?
Polyethylene
Cellulose
Silk protein
Granite

Why are plastics sorted by type before recycling?

All plastics are exactly the same
Sorting makes plastics biodegradable
Only one type of plastic can melt

Why is synthetic rubber used in many car tires?

It is grown on trees in rainforests
It dissolves when the road gets wet
It makes tires softer than paper
Chemists can adjust synthetic rubber so it grips the road and wears down slowly.
Which statement about synthetic materials is true?
Their properties can be planned by chemists
They are always found in nature unchanged
They can never be recycled at all

sciXsThermT: The burner is under a pot of water, but the water at the top gets hot too. Why?
Convection currents carry warm water upward
Radiation from the ceiling heats the top
Cold water rises and pushes heat up
The air above conducts heat downward

Water warms faster, so warm lake air flows onto land
Land cools faster, so cold air sinks over the lake

Hot smoke conducts heat to you
Cold air sinks down onto you
Sound waves carry heat from the fire
Radiation travels in straight lines from the fire and does not need moving air.

Conduction
Radiation
Reflection
Evaporation
Conduction passes energy from particle to particle where objects touch.
Why are winter jackets filled with down or fluffy fibres?
Trapped air is a poor conductor of heat
Feathers make their own heat
Fibres soak up cold from the air
Down reflects all sound waves

Why are most cooking pots made of metal?
Metals conduct heat well to the food
Metals keep heat away from food
Metals give off cold to the food
Metals stop all radiation

Why do emergency blankets have a shiny silver surface?
It reflects radiated heat back to the body
It conducts body heat away quickly
It creates convection currents
It absorbs cold from the air
A shiny surface reflects infrared radiation, so less body heat escapes.
Why is the air near the ceiling of a room usually warmer than near the floor?
Warm air is less dense and rises
Warm air is denser and rises
Cold air conducts heat upward
Radiation pushes air upward
Warmer air expands, becomes less dense and floats above cooler air.
Why are double-pane windows good at keeping heat in?
The gas layer between panes slows conduction
The two panes reflect all sunlight
The glass produces its own heat
The gap speeds up heat flow outside
Gas between the panes is a poor conductor, so less heat travels through the window.
Thermal energy always flows naturally from…
a warmer object to a cooler one
a cooler object to a warmer one
a larger object to a smaller one
a heavier object to a lighter one
Heat moves from higher to lower temperature until both are the same.
Which surface absorbs the most radiant energy from the Sun?
A dull black surface
A shiny silver surface
A glossy white surface
A smooth mirror surface
Dark, dull surfaces absorb most radiation instead of reflecting it.
Why do vacuum flasks have shiny inner walls?

The shiny walls conduct heat faster
The shiny walls add extra heat
The shiny walls cause convection
A shiny surface reflects infrared radiation, reducing heat transfer by radiation.
Ice cubes melt faster on a metal tray than on a plastic tray at room temperature. Why?
Metal conducts heat to the ice faster
Plastic conducts heat to the ice faster
Metal is colder than the room air
Plastic reflects heat onto the ice

How does the Sun's energy reach Earth?
By radiation through space
By conduction through space
By convection through space
By streams of hot air

What causes the slow movement of hot rock in Earth's mantle?
Convection currents
Reflection
Solar radiation
Wind
Hotter mantle rock rises and cooler rock sinks, forming slow convection currents.
Which material would make the best handle for a hot frying pan?
Wood
Copper
Aluminum
Iron
Wood is a poor conductor, so it keeps heat from reaching your hand.
Why does a fan oven cook food more evenly than an oven without a fan?
A fan circulates hot air around the food
It heats food only by radiation
It heats food only by touching it
It cools the outside of the food
Moving hot air spreads heat evenly by forced convection.
You touch a hot pan and burn your finger. Which transfer caused the burn?
Conduction
Radiation
Convection
Insulation
Thermal energy passed directly from the pan to your skin through contact.
Why do birds fluff up their feathers on cold days?
To trap more air, which insulates them
To catch more sunlight with each feather
To conduct body heat away faster

Which level is broader than Family but more specific than Class?
Order sits between Class and Family.
Which level is broader than Species but more specific than Family?
Genus sits between Family and Species.
Animals, plants and fungi are each an example of which level?
Animalia, Plantae and Fungi are kingdoms.
Which is the broadest level of classification?
Domain is the top, broadest level that contains the most kinds of organisms.
Which level comes right before Species (from broadest to most specific)?
Genus is the level just above Species.
Which level comes right before Family (from broadest to most specific)?
Order is the level just above Family.
Which level comes right before Class (from broadest to most specific)?
Phylum is the level just above Class.
In the scientific name Ursus americanus (black bear), what is Ursus?
A scientific name is written as genus then species, so Ursus is the genus.
A scientific name like Castor canadensis (beaver) is made of which two levels?
Binomial names give the genus followed by the species.
Which scientist created the two-part naming system for species?
Carl Linnaeus developed binomial nomenclature in the 1700s.
As you move from Kingdom toward Species, the organisms in each group become…
Lower levels contain fewer kinds of organisms that share more characteristics.
Which level contains the most different kinds of organisms?
Of these choices, Kingdom is the broadest, so it includes the most kinds of organisms.
Humans and chimpanzees are in the same family but different genera. Which level do they NOT share?
Being in different genera means they split at the Genus level while sharing all broader levels.
Wolves and domestic dogs share the genus Canis. Which other level must they also share?
Organisms in the same genus must also be in the same family and all broader levels.
How many main levels are in the classification system from Domain to Species?
The levels are Domain, Kingdom, Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus and Species.
Which of these is the correct order from broadest to most specific?
Class contains orders, and each order contains families.
Which of these is the correct order from broadest to most specific?
Kingdom is broader than Phylum, which is broader than Class.
Which of these is the correct order from most specific to broadest?
Going upward from Species, the next levels are Genus and then Family.
Which level comes two steps after Order (from broadest to most specific)?
Order is followed by Family and then Genus.
A memory trick for the levels is "Dear King Philip Came Over For Good Soup." What does "Came" stand for?
The words match Domain, Kingdom, Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus, Species, so Came is Class.
Two organisms in the same order must also be in the same…
Each order belongs to one class, so sharing an order means sharing the class too.
sciCellFn: Which cell part releases energy from food through cellular respiration?
Mitochondria break down sugar to release energy the cell can use.
Which cell part captures light energy to make food?
Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll and carry out photosynthesis.
Which cell part contains DNA and controls cell activities?
The nucleus holds the genetic material that directs the cell's activities.
Which cell part gives a plant cell a rigid shape and support?
The tough cell wall outside the membrane supports and protects plant cells.
Which cell part stores water, food and wastes?
Vacuoles are storage sacs; plant cells have a large central vacuole full of water.
Which cell part contains enzymes that break down wastes and worn-out parts?
Lysosomes hold digestive enzymes that break down unwanted materials.
Which part is the jelly-like fluid that fills the cell and holds organelles?
Cytoplasm surrounds the organelles and is where many reactions happen.
Which part inside the nucleus makes ribosomes?
The nucleolus is a dense region of the nucleus that builds ribosomes.
Which cell part is called the powerhouse of the cell?
Mitochondria release most of the cell's usable energy.
Rough endoplasmic reticulum looks bumpy because it is covered with…
Ribosomes attached to rough ER make proteins that the ER then transports.
Which cell part surrounds the nucleus and has pores?
The nuclear membrane (envelope) encloses the nucleus and has pores for materials to pass.
Which structure helps an animal cell divide by forming spindle fibres?
Centrioles help organize the spindle fibres that separate chromosomes during division.
A wilted plant has cells that have lost water from which part?
When the central vacuole loses water, cells lose pressure and the plant wilts.
Which cell part would be most common in a muscle cell that needs lots of energy?
Cells that use a lot of energy, like muscle cells, have many mitochondria.
Which cell part is selectively permeable?
The cell membrane lets some substances through and blocks others.
Which green pigment inside chloroplasts absorbs light?
Chlorophyll absorbs light energy used in photosynthesis.
Which cell part modifies proteins and sends them out in small sacs called vesicles?
The Golgi apparatus processes, packages and ships proteins in vesicles.
Which cell part makes lipids and has no ribosomes on it?
Smooth ER lacks ribosomes and makes lipids such as fats.
Which cell part would be missing in a root cell that grows underground?
Root cells get no light, so they usually have no chloroplasts.
Which structure is a network of fibres that gives the cell shape and helps it move?
The cytoskeleton is a framework of protein fibres inside the cytoplasm.
Where in the cell does photosynthesis happen?
Which cell part holds the instructions for making all of the cell's proteins?
The DNA in the nucleus carries the instructions, and ribosomes follow them to make proteins.
sciCellCmp: Which cells have a nuclear membrane?
Both plant and animal cells are eukaryotic, so their nucleus is enclosed by a membrane.
Which cells carry out cellular respiration?
Plant and animal cells both break down sugar in mitochondria to release energy.
Only plant cells contain chloroplasts, where photosynthesis happens.
Both plant and animal cells have a nucleus containing a nucleolus.
Which cells store starch made from their own sugar?
Plant cells store the sugar they make as starch; animal cells store glycogen instead.
Both plant and animal cells are filled with cytoplasm.
Which cells have a Golgi apparatus?
Both plant and animal cells package proteins with a Golgi apparatus.
Both plant and animal cells use endoplasmic reticulum to make and move materials.
Chlorophyll is found in chloroplasts, which only plant cells have.
Which cells have a wall made of cellulose?
Plant cell walls are made of cellulose; animal cells have no cell wall.
Which shape is typical of a plant cell?
The rigid cell wall gives plant cells a box-like shape.
Why do animal cells have no fixed shape?
Without a rigid cell wall, the flexible membrane lets animal cells change shape.
Which part is found in plant cells but not in animal cells?
Only plant cells contain chloroplasts for photosynthesis.
Which part is found in both plant and animal cells?
All cells have a cell membrane, but the other parts are only in plant cells.
Which part is usually found in animal cells but rarely in plant cells?
Centrioles help animal cells divide; most plant cells lack them.
How do the vacuoles of plant and animal cells compare?
Plant cells have one large one
Animal cells have one large one
Both have one very large one
Plant cells have one large central vacuole; animal cells have small ones if any.
How is a plant cell's outer boundary different from an animal cell's?
It has a wall outside the membrane
It has a membrane outside the wall
It has no membrane at all
It has no boundary at all
Plant cells have a cell wall outside their cell membrane, while animal cells have only the membrane.
How do plant and animal cells get their energy differently?
Plant cells can make their own food
Animal cells can make their own food
Plant cells make sugar by photosynthesis, while animal cells must take in food; both use mitochondria.
Which statement about mitochondria is true?
Plant and animal cells both have them
Both cell types use mitochondria to release energy from sugar.
A cell has a nucleus, mitochondria and a cell wall, but no chloroplasts. It could be a…
Only plant cells have cell walls, and root cells lack chloroplasts because they get no light.
A cell has a nucleus, mitochondria and centrioles, but no cell wall. It is most likely…
No cell wall and having centrioles both point to an animal cell.
Which pair of parts would tell you a cell is from a plant?
Cell walls and chloroplasts are found in plant cells but not animal cells.
sciXsRCIntro: What type of rock forms when heat and pressure change an existing rock?
Metamorphic rocks form when heat and pressure change rocks without melting them.
What type of rock forms when layers of sediment are pressed and cemented together?
Sedimentary rocks form from compacted and cemented sediments.
Magma is molten rock underground; it is called lava once it reaches the surface.
Which process moves rock pieces from one place to another?
Erosion carries weathered pieces away by water, wind, ice or gravity.
What must happen to a rock for it to become magma?
Rocks become magma when they get hot enough to melt deep underground.
Granite is an example of which type of rock?
Granite forms when magma cools slowly underground.
Sandstone is an example of which type of rock?
Sandstone forms from grains of sand that are pressed and cemented together.
Marble is an example of which type of rock?
Marble forms when limestone is changed by heat and pressure.
What can sedimentary rock become after being buried deep and squeezed?
Heat and pressure deep underground change sedimentary rock into metamorphic rock.
What happens to sediments before they become sedimentary rock?
Layers of sediment are pressed together and glued by minerals to form rock.
Which source of energy drives melting and metamorphism in the rock cycle?
Heat from inside Earth melts rocks and changes them under pressure.
Which source of energy drives weathering and erosion at the surface?
Sunlight drives weather, wind and the water cycle that wear down and move rock.
What type of rock forms when magma cools slowly underground?
Slow cooling underground gives crystals time to grow large.
Why do rocks formed from lava often have tiny crystals?
Fast cooling at the surface leaves little time for crystals to grow.
Which is NOT one of the three main rock types?
The three main rock types are igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic.
Can an igneous rock become a sedimentary rock?
Igneous rock can be broken into sediment, which later forms sedimentary rock.
Can a metamorphic rock become an igneous rock?
Yes, if it melts and cools
No, it can only stay metamorphic
Only if fossils form in it
If metamorphic rock melts into magma and cools, it becomes igneous rock.
Where are sediments most often deposited?
At the bottom of lakes and oceans
Water carries sediments and drops them in calm places like lake and ocean floors.
Which rock is made of shells and skeletons of sea creatures?
Limestone is a sedimentary rock that often forms from shells and skeletons.
Slate forms when which rock is changed by heat and pressure?
Shale, a sedimentary rock, becomes slate through metamorphism.
What do we call the slow, ongoing changes of rocks from one type into another?
The rock cycle describes how rocks change between igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic types.
How long do most rock cycle changes take?
Most rock cycle processes, like burial and metamorphism, are extremely slow.
sciDrift: Fossils of the plant Glossopteris are found in South America, Africa, India, Antarctica and Australia. This suggests these lands…
were connected by bridges of ice
The seeds of Glossopteris could not cross oceans, so the continents must once have been joined.
Coal, which forms from swampy forests, has been found in Antarctica. This suggests Antarctica…
was once in a warmer location
Coal forms from warm-climate plants, so Antarctica must have been closer to the equator long ago.
Scratches left by ancient glaciers are found in parts of Africa and India that are now warm. This supports the idea that…
Glaciers left these marks when the continents were joined near the South Pole, before they drifted.
Why did most scientists at first reject Wegener's idea of continental drift?
He could not explain what moved the continents
He had no fossil evidence at all
He said the Earth was flat
He thought the oceans were rising
Wegener had evidence that continents moved, but no accepted mechanism for how they moved.
Who proposed the idea of sea-floor spreading in the early 1960s?
Harry Hess suggested that new ocean floor forms at mid-ocean ridges and spreads outward.
Matching stripes of magnetic rock on both sides of a mid-ocean ridge show that…
new sea floor forms and spreads
the ridge is made of iron
Rock records Earth's magnetic field as it forms, so mirror-image stripes show spreading from the ridge.
Which Canadian scientist helped develop plate tectonics with ideas about hot spots and transform faults?
J. Tuzo Wilson, a Canadian geophysicist, explained hot spot island chains and transform faults.
Mountains in eastern North America match mountains of the same age and rock type in…
The Appalachians match old mountains in the British Isles and Scandinavia that were joined in Pangaea.
Pangaea first split into which two large landmasses?
Pangaea broke into Laurasia in the north and Gondwana in the south.
About how fast do tectonic plates move?
Plates move only a few centimetres a year, about as fast as fingernails grow.
Which tool lets scientists measure plate movement directly today?
GPS receivers on the ground track tiny changes in position over years.
Most earthquakes and volcanoes are found…
in the middle of every plate
The pattern of earthquakes and volcanoes outlines the edges of the plates.
Fossils of the reptile Lystrosaurus are found in Africa, India and Antarctica. Why is this evidence of drift?
It could not swim across oceans
It lived only in deep oceans
It lived only in very cold places
A land animal could not cross wide oceans, so these lands must have been connected.
The layer under the plates that flows slowly and lets them move is the…
The plates of the lithosphere move over the soft, slowly flowing asthenosphere.
The rigid outer layer broken into tectonic plates is the…
The lithosphere, made of crust and upper mantle, is broken into plates.
Sediment on the ocean floor is thinnest…
Rock at the ridges is new, so it has had little time to collect sediment.
Wegener's theory of continental drift was published in about…
Wegener published his ideas in 1915 in a book on the origin of continents and oceans.
In which direction is the Atlantic Ocean changing in size?
Sea-floor spreading at the Mid-Atlantic Ridge pushes the Americas away from Europe and Africa.
Which observation shows that Hawaii's islands formed as a plate moved over a hot spot?
The islands get older in a line
All the islands are the same age
The islands are made of granite
As the Pacific Plate moves, each new island forms over the hot spot, leaving older ones farther away.
Rocks of the same type and age line up across the Atlantic in Brazil and western Africa. This suggests…
the rocks were carried by rivers
Matching rock formations on separate continents show they were once one landmass.
The theory that Earth's outer layer is made of moving plates is called…
Plate tectonics combines continental drift and sea-floor spreading into one theory.
Where is old ocean floor destroyed as plates move?
At subduction zones, ocean plates sink back into the mantle, balancing new crust made at ridges.
sciXsPlateLbl: Which boundary is shown when two plates slide past each other sideways?
At transform boundaries, plates grind past each other horizontally.
Which boundary is shown when two plates move toward each other?
Convergent boundaries are where plates collide or one sinks beneath another.
What is the zone called where one plate sinks beneath another?
In a subduction zone, the denser plate dives down into the mantle.
Which plate usually sinks when an ocean plate meets a continental plate?
The ocean plate, because it is denser
The continental plate, because it is denser
Both plates, at the same speed
Oceanic crust is denser than continental crust, so it subducts.
What landform is a long, narrow, very deep valley in the ocean floor at a subduction zone?
Trenches form where one plate bends down beneath another.
What kind of mountains form when rock layers are squeezed and bent at a collision?
Compression at convergent boundaries folds rock layers into mountains.
A line of volcanoes on land next to an ocean trench is called a…
Melting of the sinking plate feeds a curved line of volcanoes called a volcanic arc.
A chain of islands that gets older in one direction most likely formed over a…
A plate moving over a fixed hot spot leaves a line of volcanoes of increasing age.
An underwater mountain chain with a crack down its centre is a…
Mid-ocean ridges form where plates pull apart and magma rises to make new crust.
Which feature is found at a transform boundary?
Plates sliding past each other create long faults with frequent earthquakes.
Why do volcanoes form above subduction zones?
The sinking plate helps rock melt
Water from the sinking plate lowers the melting point of the mantle, forming magma that rises.
Which boundary usually has volcanoes, deep trenches and strong earthquakes?
Subduction of an ocean plate under a continent produces trenches, volcanoes and big earthquakes.
Why are there few volcanoes where two continental plates collide?
The plates are too cold to move
Continental crust is too light to subduct deeply, so little magma forms; mountains rise instead.
What fills the gap where two plates pull apart at a ridge?
Magma that cools into new crust
Magma rises into the gap, cools and forms new oceanic crust.
Which type of boundary is also called a constructive boundary because crust is made there?
New crust forms at divergent boundaries, so they are called constructive.
Which type of boundary destroys crust as one plate sinks?
At convergent subduction zones, crust sinks into the mantle and is destroyed.
At which boundary is crust neither made nor destroyed?
At transform boundaries, plates only slide past each other.
What is the point inside Earth where an earthquake starts called?
The focus is where rock first breaks; the epicentre is the point on the surface above it.
A diagram shows arrows pointing away from each other at a crack in the ocean floor. Which feature is it?
Plates moving apart under the ocean form a mid-ocean ridge.
A diagram shows arrows pointing toward each other and one plate going under the other. Which feature forms at the bend?
Where one plate bends down beneath another, a deep trench forms.
A diagram shows arrows pointing opposite ways along a straight line on land. What does it label?
Opposite sideways motion along a line is a transform fault.
What is the point on Earth's surface directly above an earthquake's starting point?
The epicentre lies directly above the focus.
sciXsPlateWld: The Hawaiian Islands formed mainly over a…
Hawaii sits in the middle of the Pacific Plate above a hot spot.
The Mariana Trench formed at a…
The Pacific Plate sinks beneath another plate there, forming the deepest trench.
The Alps in Europe formed where…
The African Plate moving north into the Eurasian Plate pushed up the Alps.
The Red Sea is slowly widening at a…
The Arabian Plate is pulling away from Africa, widening the Red Sea.
The Queen Charlotte Fault, off Haida Gwaii in British Columbia, is mainly a…
Along this fault, the Pacific Plate slides past the North American Plate.
Which small plate sinks beneath North America off the coast of British Columbia?
The Juan de Fuca Plate subducts under the North American Plate at the Cascadia subduction zone.
Mount St. Helens and the other Cascade volcanoes formed because…
an ocean plate subducts beneath North America
two plates pull apart in Washington
a hot spot sits under the volcanoes
Melting above the subducting Juan de Fuca Plate feeds the Cascade volcanoes.
Most of Canada sits on which tectonic plate?
Canada lies almost entirely on the North American Plate.
Iceland is being pulled apart by which two plates?
The Mid-Atlantic Ridge runs through Iceland, separating the North American and Eurasian plates.
The Andes form where which plate sinks beneath South America?
The oceanic Nazca Plate subducts beneath the South American Plate.
The Aleutian Islands of Alaska are an island arc formed by…
The Pacific Plate sinking under the North American Plate created the arc of volcanic islands.
Why is Mount Everest still getting slightly taller?
A hot spot pushes it upward
Glaciers add rock to its top
The ongoing collision of the Indian and Eurasian plates continues to lift the Himalayas.
The strongest earthquake ever recorded, in Chile in 1960, happened at a…
It struck where the Nazca Plate subducts beneath South America.
The East Pacific Rise is an example of a…
The East Pacific Rise is a mid-ocean ridge where plates spread apart.
Yellowstone National Park sits above a…
Yellowstone's geysers and past eruptions come from a hot spot under the North American Plate.
Why are earthquakes common in California?
Two plates slide past each other there
A hot spot lies under it
It sits in the middle of a plate
The Pacific Plate grinds past the North American Plate along the San Andreas Fault.
Which country is crossed by the North Anatolian Fault, a major transform boundary?
The North Anatolian Fault in Turkey is a transform fault with frequent earthquakes.
Mount Fuji in Japan formed mainly because of…
Japan's volcanoes form above plates that subduct beneath it.
The Ring of Fire is mostly made of which kind of boundary?
Most of the Ring of Fire is subduction zones that produce volcanoes and earthquakes.
The Atlantic coast of Canada is quiet geologically because it…
is far from any plate boundary
Eastern Canada is in the middle of the North American Plate, away from active boundaries.
Which plate is moving north into Asia to form the Himalayas?
The Indian Plate's collision with the Eurasian Plate built the Himalayas.
The Great Rift Valley in East Africa may one day become…
As the African continent splits apart, seawater may eventually flood the rift, as it did in the Red Sea.
sciXsWCSel: Which process returns water from clouds to Earth's surface?
Precipitation is water falling from clouds as rain, snow, sleet or hail.
A puddle disappears on a sunny afternoon. Which process happened?
Heat from the Sun turned the liquid water into water vapour.
Water droplets form on the outside of a cold glass of juice. Which process is this?
Water vapour in the air cools on the cold glass and turns into liquid.
Rainwater flows over a parking lot into a storm drain. Which process is this?
Water that flows over the ground surface instead of soaking in is runoff.
Which process turns water vapour directly into frost on a cold window?
Deposition is when a gas changes straight into a solid, as when vapour forms frost.
Snow on a mountain turns into liquid water in spring. Which process is this?
Melting changes solid ice or snow into liquid water.
What provides the energy that drives the water cycle?
Sunlight heats water and causes evaporation, which keeps the cycle moving.
Where is most of Earth's water found?
About 97% of Earth's water is salt water in the oceans.
An underground layer of rock or gravel that holds water is called…
Aquifers store groundwater in the spaces in rock, sand or gravel.
Fog forming over a lake on a cool morning is an example of…
Fog is tiny water droplets made when water vapour cools near the ground.
Water absorbed by tree roots exits through tiny holes in the leaves. Which process is this?
Transpiration is the release of water vapour from plant leaves.
In a diagram, an arrow goes from a lake up to a cloud. What process does it show?
Water moving from a lake into the air as vapour is evaporation.
In a diagram, an arrow goes from a cloud down to a mountain. What process does it show?
Water falling from a cloud to the ground is precipitation.
In a diagram, an arrow goes from a hillside into the soil below. What process does it show?
Water soaking down into the ground is infiltration.
In a diagram, an arrow goes from a tree's leaves up into the air. What process does it show?
Water vapour leaving plant leaves is transpiration.
Snow falling on the Prairies in January is an example of…
Snow is a form of precipitation falling from clouds.
Which process is more likely on a paved road than on a grassy field?
Pavement stops water from soaking in, so more of it runs off the surface.
Rain falling on a forest soaks into loose soil. Which process is this?
Infiltration is water entering and moving down into the soil.
Snow slowly shrinks on a cold, sunny, windy day without melting. Which process is this?
Sublimation is solid ice changing directly into water vapour.
Which process makes water vapour turn into tiny cloud droplets high in the sky?
As air rises and cools, water vapour condenses into droplets that form clouds.
Melted snow flowing downhill into a river in spring is an example of…
Meltwater moving over the surface into streams and rivers is runoff.
What do we call water stored below ground that fills spaces in soil and rock?
Groundwater is water held underground in soil and rock.
sciXsCarbon: In which form is carbon found in the atmosphere?
Most carbon in the air is in the gas carbon dioxide, CO<sub>2</sub>.
How do animals get the carbon they need to build their bodies?
By eating plants or other animals
By soaking it up from sunlight
Consumers get carbon compounds from the food they eat.
Which process releases carbon dioxide when living things use food for energy?
Cellular respiration breaks down sugar and releases CO<sub>2</sub> as a waste product.
Fossil fuels such as coal and oil formed from…
the remains of ancient living things
Buried plants and tiny sea organisms were changed by heat and pressure over millions of years.
Which organisms break down dead matter and release carbon back to the air and soil?
Decomposers such as fungi and bacteria break down dead matter and release CO<sub>2</sub>.
Which natural event releases carbon from deep inside Earth into the air?
Volcanoes release carbon dioxide gas from Earth's interior.
shells and skeletons of sea creatures
Sea creatures build shells from carbon compounds, which pile up and become limestone.
Which gas, produced by burning fossil fuels, traps heat in the atmosphere?
Carbon dioxide is a greenhouse gas that traps heat and warms Earth.
What happens to ocean water as it absorbs more carbon dioxide?
CO<sub>2</sub> reacts with water to form carbonic acid, lowering the ocean's pH.
Which Canadian ecosystem stores large amounts of carbon in its trees, peat and soil?
Canada's boreal forest and peatlands hold huge amounts of carbon in plants and soil.
Which pair of processes are opposites in the carbon cycle?
Photosynthesis takes in CO<sub>2</sub>, while respiration releases it.
In photosynthesis, plants combine carbon dioxide and water to make…
Plants use light energy to turn CO<sub>2</sub> and water into glucose and oxygen.
Which of these is a carbon source rather than a carbon sink?
Burning coal releases more carbon than it stores, so it is a source.
Which action would help reduce the amount of carbon dioxide added to the air?
Using transit instead of a car burns less fuel, so less CO<sub>2</sub> is released.
Which holds more carbon: the oceans or the atmosphere?
The oceans store many times more carbon than the atmosphere.
Why does thawing permafrost in northern Canada worry scientists?
It removes carbon from the air
As frozen soil thaws, microbes break down old plant matter and release CO<sub>2</sub> and methane.
Carbon atoms in a maple leaf came most directly from…
Plants build their tissues from carbon taken from CO<sub>2</sub> during photosynthesis.
Which carbon-containing gas is released by cows during digestion?
Microbes in a cow's stomach produce methane, which is also a greenhouse gas.
Burning a log in a campfire releases carbon as…
Combustion combines the carbon in wood with oxygen to make CO<sub>2</sub>.
Which part of a living thing is made from carbon compounds?
Sugars, fats, proteins and DNA are all built around carbon atoms.
Why do carbon dioxide levels in the air rise slightly in the Northern Hemisphere winter?
Leaves fall and plants slow down in winter, so less CO<sub>2</sub> is taken from the air.
What is the movement of carbon between the air, living things, oceans and rocks called?
The carbon cycle describes how carbon moves among Earth's reservoirs.
